unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: After PEEP increases, saturation rises but arterial pressure falls. Which response best fits the combined observations?

choice.label: Accept the change because saturation improved
choice.rationale: This overlooks a potentially important circulatory cost.

learnerFacingSafety.current: Higher PEEP raises pressure in the chest, which can reduce venous return and cardiac output; the falling arterial pressure is the warning that this may be happening. Oxygen reaching the tissues depends on cardiac output as well as saturation, so it can fall while saturation rises, and accepting the change on saturation alone keeps that PEEP in place.

items.teachingPoint: An oxygenation gain from higher PEEP is judged with its circulatory cost: falling arterial pressure warns that cardiac output may be lower, and oxygen delivery can fall while saturation rises.

sourceLocators.statement: A rise in intrathoracic pressure from PEEP can lower cardiac output, largely by reducing venous return
sourceLocators.note: With poor left-ventricular function, cardiac output is relatively insensitive to lower venous return; the notes say “can”.

sourceLocators.statement: Positive airway pressure lowers cardiac output by reducing cardiac filling
sourceLocators.note: Stated for positive airway pressure generally, not only PEEP.

sourceLocators.statement: A fall in cardiac output with PEEP is inevitable
sourceLocators.note: The effect depends strongly on intravascular volume and volume expansion can restore cardiac output; neither note says the fall is inevitable.

sourceLocators.statement: A PEEP-induced rise in arterial oxygen content can be accompanied by a fall in oxygen delivery because cardiac output falls
sourceLocators.note: The same section reports patients with severe ARDS in whom higher PEEP raised cardiac output and oxygen delivery, so the direction depends on the patient; the notes say “can” and “may”.

sourceLocators.statement: A falling arterial pressure after a PEEP increase is the bedside warning to weigh the circulatory cost
sourceLocators.note: The chapter gives the mechanism and its effect on oxygen delivery; treating the blood-pressure fall as the bedside warning is this module’s reasoning.

unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: A patient’s oxygen saturation rises after a pressure adjustment, while perfusion worsens. What best describes this response?

choice.label: A successful change demonstrated by the saturation
choice.rationale: That interpretation overlooks the worsening perfusion.

learnerFacingSafety.current: Worsening perfusion means less blood may be carrying oxygen to the tissues. A pressure change that raises saturation can also lower cardiac output, and oxygen delivery depends on both, so it can fall even as saturation improves. Calling the change a success on saturation alone would keep, or build on, a setting that may be reducing oxygen delivery.

items.teachingPoint: Worsening perfusion after a pressure change that raises saturation means oxygen delivery may be falling, so saturation alone cannot show the change succeeded.

unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: A patient develops an alarm, new hypoxemia, hypotension, and asymmetric breath sounds. Which priority best fits?

choice.label: Finish waveform classification before calling for help
choice.rationale: This delays stabilization of a deteriorating patient.

learnerFacingSafety.current: New hypoxemia with hypotension can be fatal within minutes if the cause is not found and treated, and asymmetric breath sounds point to causes found at the bedside, such as a pneumothorax or a tube that has moved into the right main bronchus. Classifying the waveform before calling for help delays the support and bedside checks this patient needs now.

items.teachingPoint: New hypoxemia and hypotension with asymmetric breath sounds is time-critical: support and bedside checks for a pneumothorax or tube position come before classifying the waveform.

unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: A patient develops an alarm, new hypoxemia, hypotension, and asymmetric breath sounds. Which priority best fits?

choice.label: Acknowledge the alarm and observe for improvement
choice.rationale: Acknowledgment does not treat the cause of instability.

learnerFacingSafety.current: Acknowledging the alarm changes only the warning; the hypoxemia, hypotension and asymmetric breath sounds are still there. Possible causes such as a pneumothorax or a displaced tube have to be found and treated, and in a patient this unstable, minutes spent watching for improvement can be fatal.

items.teachingPoint: Acknowledging an alarm changes the warning, not the patient; unstable findings with asymmetric breath sounds need their cause found and treated now, not watched.

items.decisionNeeded: Faculty/RT decisions on: (1) which alarm and limit the stem means, since it names none; (2) wording that separates re-setting limits around verified, acceptable readings, which the HAMILTON-C6 and Evita manuals provide as an automatic function, from widening a limit around an unresolved abnormality; (3) whether to say that on several registered ventilators the high-pressure limit also caps or ends the breath, so raising it changes ventilation as well as the warning; (4) whether this choice and the MV-03 alarm-limit note should share one sourced wording. unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: A new high-pressure alarm occurs with abrupt hypotension and asymmetric breath sounds. Which next priority is most appropriate?

choice.label: Wait for a relaxed plateau before requesting assistance
choice.rationale: A deteriorating patient cannot wait for a perfect mechanics measurement.

learnerFacingSafety.current: A high-pressure alarm with abrupt hypotension and asymmetric breath sounds raises concern for a tension pneumothorax, and a patient this unstable may die within minutes if the cause is not treated. A plateau is worth measuring when possible, but waiting for a relaxed one before asking for help delays the support and treatment that come first.

items.teachingPoint: High pressure, abrupt hypotension and asymmetric breath sounds raise concern for a tension pneumothorax; help and support come before waiting for a relaxed plateau.
